title: Roberto Goizueta becomes chairman of Coca-Cola
what: Roberto Goizueta, a Cuban-born, Yale-trained chemical engineer who started with the Coca-Cola bottler in Cuba in 1954, became chairman of Coca-Cola in March, succeeding J. Paul Austin. He has already been president and chief executive since August 1980.
why: Goizueta ran the company until his death in 1997 and made shareholder value its stated goal; a 1,000 dollar investment in 1981 grew to about 62,000 dollars with dividends by 1997.

title: Goizueta's two bets: Columbia Pictures and Diet Coke
what: Coca-Cola unveiled Diet Coke on 8 July and launched it in New York City; it is to reach most of the United States by the end of the year. It is the first new product to carry the Coca-Cola trademark since 1886. Last month the company agreed to buy the Hollywood studio Columbia Pictures for about 750 million dollars, a controversial move: chairman Goizueta argues entertainment has good growth prospects and can use Coca-Cola's skill in market research. Pepsi has been gaining market share in soft drinks.
why: Diet Coke became the most successful consumer product launch of the 1980s and proved the Coke name could be stretched, which emboldened the company for New Coke. Columbia ended well financially: Coca-Cola sold its stake to Sony in 1989 and made about a billion dollars on the venture.

title: Diet Coke takes off; Columbia earns more than expected
what: Coca-Cola's net income rose 9% to 559 million dollars in 1983 on revenue of 6.8 billion. Diet Coke, launched only in July 1982, captured 17% of the fast-growing US diet soft drink market by the end of 1983 and became the fourth best-selling soft drink in North America; it has been introduced in 28 markets abroad. Columbia Pictures' profits in its first full year were well above expectations. Coca-Cola products make up more than 35% of the soft drinks drunk worldwide.
why: Goizueta's early years: steady growth and successful bets, while the share price rose only modestly in 1983 and 1984.

title: Coca-Cola changes its formula: New Coke
what: On 23 April Coca-Cola replaced its 99-year-old formula with a sweeter new one. The company says the sweeter drink beat both the old Coke and Pepsi in blind taste tests. Pepsi now has a slightly bigger share of the US market than Coca-Cola's flagship. The company hotline is getting more than 1,500 calls a day, up from about 400, many of them angry.
why: The most famous marketing blunder of the decade, and one of the few public missteps of the Goizueta era. The stock barely suffered.

title: Old Coke comes back as Coca-Cola Classic
what: On 11 July, 79 days after the change, Coca-Cola announced that the original formula will return under the name Coca-Cola Classic, sold next to the new Coke. The company had received more than 40,000 angry calls and letters. Sales had actually been up 8% on the year before.
why: The retreat turned into free publicity: by the end of 1985 Coca-Cola Classic was outselling both New Coke and Pepsi. The shares gained about 42% in 1985.

title: Coca-Cola floats its bottlers as Coca-Cola Enterprises
what: Coca-Cola bought the two largest US bottling groups this year, from the Lupton family's JTL for 1.4 billion dollars and from Beatrice for 1 billion, and put them into a new company, Coca-Cola Enterprises. It sold 51% of it to the public in the largest first share sale in US history so far, raising about 1.5 billion dollars, and keeps 49%. That takes the 2.4 billion dollars of borrowing for the purchases off Coca-Cola's own books.
why: The model of the next 30 years: Coca-Cola owns the brands and the syrup, while capital-hungry bottling sits in separate, partly owned companies. Coca-Cola bought the North American part back in 2010 and sold the territories again by 2017.

title: Crash, and Coca-Cola reshapes its film business
what: Coca-Cola shares lost about 15% in October as stock markets crashed on 19 October. In September Coca-Cola agreed to sell its entertainment business, Columbia Pictures, to Tri-Star Pictures, of which it owned 30%, in return for raising its stake in the combined company to 80%. Coca-Cola joined the Dow Jones Industrial Average this year.
why: The crash was a market move; Coca-Cola fell less than the market and recovered with it. The Tri-Star deal was the first step out of Hollywood, completed with the sale to Sony in 1989.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Monday_(1987) (read 2026-10-03); https://www.company-histories.com/The-CocaCola-Company-Company-History.html (Tri-Star deal, read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Coca-Cola_Company (Dow membership since 1987, read 2026-10-03); move from data/out/ko.json

title: Warren Buffett reveals a big stake in Coca-Cola
what: Berkshire Hathaway's annual letter shows that it bought 14,172,500 Coca-Cola shares in 1988 for 592.5 million dollars, worth 632.4 million at the end of the year. Warren Buffett writes that he expects to hold the stake for a long time. Coca-Cola earned more than a billion dollars in 1988, a goal Goizueta had set for 1990.
why: Buffett's endorsement and continued buying (23.35 million shares by the end of 1989) became part of the stock's story; 1989 was one of Coca-Cola's best years, with a total return of 76%.

title: Sony buys Columbia Pictures, including Coca-Cola's stake
what: On 27 September Sony agreed to buy Columbia Pictures Entertainment for 3.4 billion dollars plus 1.4 billion of debt, paying 27 dollars a share in cash for Coca-Cola's 49% stake. Coca-Cola bought Columbia in 1982 and merged it with Tri-Star in 1987. It plans to use much of the proceeds to invest in its bottling system and to buy back its own shares.
why: The end of the entertainment detour; from here Coca-Cola was a pure beverage company, and its buybacks were a big part of the 1990s earnings growth.

title: Coca-Cola's best year: 76% return in 1989, a split and a bigger dividend
what: Coca-Cola's net income per share rose 73% in 1989 to 4.92 dollars, helped by the Columbia gain, and the total return to shareholders was 76%. The board raised the dividend 18%, the largest increase since 1960, and recommends a two-for-one stock split. Over the 1980s the share price rose almost sevenfold and the market value grew from 4.3 to 26 billion dollars.
why: Sets up the 1990s, when Coca-Cola became one of the most valuable companies in America.

title: Rate cut sends blue chips soaring; Coca-Cola up 16% in a month
what: In December the Federal Reserve cut its discount rate by a full percentage point, from 4.5% to 3.5%, after a string of smaller cuts this year. Stocks surged and the S&P 500 gained about 11% in the month. Coca-Cola gained about 16%; over the year its share price rose nearly 73%, almost three times as much as the S&P 500.
why: A market move amplified by Coca-Cola's reputation as a steady grower; after 1991 the shares marked time for two years.
source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/INTDSRUSM193N (discount rate 4.5% in November 1991, 3.5% from late December, read 2026-10-03); https://archive.org/download/cocacolacoannualreports/cocacola1991_djvu.txt (1991 share price gain, read 2026-10-03); moves from data/out/ko.json and data/reference/sp500.json

title: Earnings up 20% in 1992, but the stock only kept pace
what: Coca-Cola's earnings per share and operating income rose 20% in 1992 (excluding accounting changes), after 19% in 1991, and its share of world soft drink sales reached a record 43%. Volume growth slowed to 3% as recessions hit markets such as Brazil. The share price rose only 4.4%, in line with the market, for a total return of 5.8% after 75% in 1991; the company says it is 'downright unhappy'. The board raised the quarterly dividend 21%.
why: Large growth stocks were out of favour in 1992-93; Coca-Cola's business kept compounding and the shares caught up in 1995-97.

title: Two flat years for Coca-Cola shares
what: Coca-Cola's total return to shareholders was about 8% in 1993 after about 6% in 1992, short of its record, the company admits. Its business keeps growing: it is now the fourth-largest US company by market value and the largest consumer goods company, worth about 56 billion dollars at the end of 1993. In 1993 it launched the 'Always Coca-Cola' advertising theme worldwide.
why: A pause after the shares gained more than 70% in 1991. The 'Marlboro Friday' scare of April 1993, when Philip Morris cut cigarette prices, made investors doubt branded goods for a while.

title: Coca-Cola worth 93 billion dollars after a 46% year
what: Coca-Cola's shares rose 44% in 1995, ahead of the S&P 500, for a total return of 46%. Its market value reached nearly 93 billion dollars, up 27 billion in a year. Net income rose 17% to almost 3 billion dollars. The company has bought back large amounts of its own shares, which it says lifted earnings per share growth to 18% a year.
why: The heart of the great run of the mid-1990s: investors paid ever higher multiples for Coca-Cola's steady global growth, which made the stock vulnerable when growth faltered in 1998.

title: Asian currency crisis hits Coca-Cola and other multinationals
what: Since Thailand let its currency fall in July, the crisis has spread through Southeast Asia, and the dollar has jumped against Asian currencies. Shares of multinationals like Coca-Cola, Gillette, General Electric and McDonald's fell in August on worries that slower growth in Asia and the strong dollar will eat into their earnings. Coca-Cola shares lost about 17% in the month.
why: The first crack in the premium the market paid for global consumer brands; Coca-Cola makes most of its profit abroad.

title: Roberto Goizueta dies; Douglas Ivester takes over
what: Roberto Goizueta, Coca-Cola's chairman and chief executive since 1980/81, died of lung cancer on 18 October, aged 65. On 23 October the board elected Douglas Ivester, his long-time finance chief and president, as chairman and chief executive. Under Goizueta, revenue grew from 4.8 billion dollars in 1981 to 18.5 billion in 1996 and the company's market value from 4.3 billion to about 147 billion.
why: The end of the golden era. Ivester inherited a company priced for perfection just as the world economy turned against it.

title: Russia's collapse drags Coca-Cola down
what: Russia devalued the rouble and defaulted on its government bonds in mid-August, and world stock markets fell hard; the Dow lost 357 points on 27 August alone. About three quarters of Coca-Cola's profit comes from abroad, and the company has invested heavily in Russia and Asia, where currencies have collapsed. Coca-Cola shares, which hit a record of nearly 89 dollars in mid-July, lost about 19% in August.
why: The start of Coca-Cola's long slide: the shares peaked in mid-1998 and did not regain that level for years (worst stretch -54% to November 2004). Russian sales fell about 60% from August 1998 to September 1999.

title: Coca-Cola shares rebound after results come in as warned
what: Coca-Cola reported third-quarter profit of 888 million dollars, down 12% on a year earlier, with worldwide volume up only 3%. The result was in line with what executives told analysts at an unusual meeting in September, when they warned that the crises in Asia, Russia and Latin America were hurting the business. The Federal Reserve cut its key interest rate on 29 September and again, between meetings, on 15 October, to 5%, and stocks recovered. With the bad news known, Coca-Cola shares gained about 17% in October.
why: A relief rally in a roller-coaster year: up 33% by July, down 40%, back up and down again, ending 1998 almost unchanged, as Ivester later wrote.

title: Belgian schoolchildren fall ill: Coca-Cola's biggest recall
what: Dozens of schoolchildren in Belgium became ill after drinking Coca-Cola products, and about 250 consumers in Belgium and France reported illnesses. Belgium and France temporarily banned the company's drinks and Coca-Cola recalled about 14 million cases in five European countries, the largest recall in its history. The drinks came from plants run by Coca-Cola Enterprises. Critics say the company was slow to take it seriously and apologise.
why: A public-relations disaster that added to the impression of a company that had lost its touch under Ivester.
source: https://www.company-histories.com/The-CocaCola-Company-Company-History.html (read 2026-10-03; it misdates the scare to 1998); https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1999-sep-04-fi-6777-story.html (June date, 250 consumers, read 2026-10-03)

title: Coca-Cola warns: fourth quarterly profit decline in a row
what: On 3 September Coca-Cola warned that third-quarter earnings will fall short of forecasts, at 34 to 35 cents a share against 36 expected, because of weak sales abroad and higher marketing costs, and that the European recall will cut another 2 to 3 cents. It would be the fourth straight quarter of lower earnings. In June chairman Ivester had said 'the worst is behind us.' The shares lost about 19% in September.
why: The warning destroyed what was left of Ivester's credibility with investors.

title: Coca-Cola shares bounce as key markets recover
what: Coca-Cola reported on 21 October that third-quarter profit fell 11% to 787 million dollars, the fourth decline in a row, but said sales in Japan, Mexico, Brazil and the United States, four of its five biggest markets, were 'very encouraging' and that most European markets were back to their levels before the recall. It also plans to refresh the Coca-Cola Classic look and bring back the 'Enjoy' slogan in 2000. The shares, down 20% for the year before the results, gained about 22% in October.
why: A rebound from an oversold level, which faded again within two months when Ivester quit.

title: Ivester to retire after two and a half years
what: Coca-Cola surprised investors in December by announcing that chairman and chief executive Douglas Ivester will retire in early 2000, after only about two and a half years in charge and seven quarters of falling earnings. Douglas Daft, an Australian who has spent 30 years with the company and runs its Middle and Far East and Africa business, was named president and is to take over as chairman and chief executive. The shares lost about 13% in December.
why: Daft's first move was the biggest job cut in the company's history.

title: Investors dump 'old economy' stocks: Coca-Cola down 16% this year
what: On 25 February the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed below 10,000 for the first time in nearly 11 months, nearly 16% below its January record, while the technology-heavy Nasdaq hit new highs. Investors are selling slow-growing 'old economy' blue chips to buy technology shares, and rising interest rates add to the pressure. Coca-Cola shares were down 16% for the year by 25 February; they lost about 15% in the month. In January new president Douglas Daft announced the biggest job cuts in the company's history, about 6,000 jobs or a fifth of the workforce, to make the company less centralised.
why: The low point of the dot-com rotation. Consumer staples recovered once the technology bubble burst from March 2000. The job cuts were later scaled back to about 5,200 and cost about 1.6 billion dollars in charges.

title: Coca-Cola walks away from Quaker Oats and settles a race lawsuit
what: In November Coca-Cola's board pulled out of a tentative 15.75 billion dollar deal to buy Quaker Oats, the owner of the Gatorade sports drink, mainly because the price was too high. In the same month it agreed to pay 192.5 million dollars to settle a class action by African American employees, and to let an outside task force oversee its employment practices.
why: PepsiCo bought Quaker Oats instead for 13.4 billion dollars and with it Gatorade, a gap in Coca-Cola's line-up for years.

title: Daft's recovery year: earnings per share up 82%
what: Coca-Cola reported that worldwide volume rose 4% in 2001 and earnings per share grew 82%, recovering from the restructuring charges of 2000; return on equity rose from 23% to 38%. Chairman Douglas Daft says North America is growing solidly again. The shares nevertheless fell about a fifth during 2001.
why: Earnings recovered, but investors no longer paid the old premium; the shares kept sliding until 2004.
source: https://archive.org/download/cocacolacoannualreports/cocacola2001_djvu.txt (2001 annual report, read 2026-10-03); yearly change from data/out/ko.json

title: Coca-Cola cuts another 1,000 jobs
what: Coca-Cola is cutting another 1,000 jobs, half of them at its Atlanta headquarters. Its carbonated drinks are growing slowly while juices, waters and teas grow fast, and Diet Coke with Lemon and Vanilla Coke, launched in 2001 and 2002, have been its main new products.
why: The Daft years: no disaster, but no return to the old growth; the shares drifted lower until 2004.

title: Neville Isdell called back to run Coca-Cola
what: On 4 May Coca-Cola named E. Neville Isdell chairman and chief executive elect, to succeed Douglas Daft by early summer. Isdell, an Irish citizen who grew up in Africa, spent decades at Coca-Cola opening new markets before leaving in 1998 to head a big bottler, and retired in 2001. The board had looked at several outsiders.
why: A turnaround hire: Isdell soon told investors that the company had been underinvesting in its brands and cut its growth targets.

title: Isdell lowers Coca-Cola's long-term growth targets
what: After warning in September that second-half results would fall short, Coca-Cola on 11 November cut its long-term targets to volume growth of 3 to 4% a year, operating income growth of 6 to 8% and earnings per share growth in the high single digits. It will spend 350 to 400 million dollars more each year on marketing and innovation, and expects weak results in some key markets to continue into 2005.
why: The bottom: the share price in November 2004 was 54% below its June 1998 level. Resetting expectations allowed a slow recovery from 2005.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/21344/000002134404000183/ko8k1111x99-1.txt (press release of 11 November 2004, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/21344/000002134404000138/ko8k9150499-1.txt (warning of 15 September 2004, read 2026-10-03)

title: Isdell's first full year: 20 billion cases
what: Coca-Cola reported on 7 February that worldwide unit case volume grew 4% in 2005, at the top of its long-term target, and passed 20 billion cases a year for the first time. Revenue grew 6% and the company returned 4.7 billion dollars to shareholders in dividends and buybacks.
why: The slow recovery under Isdell; the shares started to climb in 2006 after six flat-to-falling years.

title: Coca-Cola buys vitaminwater maker Glaceau
what: On 25 May Coca-Cola announced it will buy Glaceau, the maker of vitaminwater, flavoured waters and Burn energy drinks, for 4.1 billion dollars in cash, its biggest purchase in years.
why: Part of the push into non-carbonated drinks as soda consumption stagnated in rich countries.

title: The financial crisis: even Coca-Cola falls 17%
what: Stock markets crashed worldwide in October as the financial crisis deepened after Lehman Brothers' failure in September. Coca-Cola shares lost about 17%, as much as the S&P 500. Muhtar Kent became chief executive on 1 July. In September Coca-Cola offered 2.4 billion dollars for China Huiyuan Juice, the leader in Chinese fruit juice.
why: A market move. Coca-Cola recovered faster than the market: by the end of 2009 its shares were above their September 2008 level. China blocked the Huiyuan bid in March 2009.

title: Coca-Cola to buy back its North American bottler
what: Coca-Cola is in talks, announced on 24 February, to buy the North American business of its biggest bottler, Coca-Cola Enterprises, which delivers about three quarters of Coca-Cola's US bottler volume and almost all in Canada. In return CCE would take over Coca-Cola's own bottling operations in Norway and Sweden.
why: Reverses the 1986 model in North America; Coca-Cola closed the deal in October 2010 and began selling the territories off again to independent bottlers from 2013.

title: Coca-Cola at 125: a billion more cases in a year
what: Coca-Cola, which celebrates 125 years in 2011, reported that its unit case volume grew 5% in 2010, adding more than a billion cases, and that it beat its long-term targets for volume and operating income. It now has more than 500 brands and closed the purchase of Coca-Cola Enterprises' North American business in October. Its '2020 Vision' plan, unveiled in 2009, sets the goals for the decade.
why: The steady Kent years: emerging markets and still drinks drove growth and the shares rose gently.

title: Coca-Cola: 16 billion-dollar brands and a stock split
what: Coca-Cola's net operating revenue passed 48 billion dollars in 2012 and operating income was nearly 11 billion; it returned 9.1 billion dollars to shareholders and announced its 51st consecutive annual dividend increase. In July 2012 it split its stock two-for-one, the first split in 16 years. Two Japanese drinks became billion-dollar brands, bringing the total to 16.
why: A mature compounder; the shares went sideways from 2013 to 2016.

title: Coca-Cola buys a 16.7% stake in Monster Beverage
what: On 14 August Coca-Cola said it will pay 2.15 billion dollars for 16.7% of Monster Beverage, the energy drink maker, with an option to go to 25%. Coca-Cola hands its own energy drinks to Monster, which in turn passes its non-energy drinks to Coca-Cola, and Coca-Cola's bottlers will distribute Monster.
why: A cheap way into the fastest-growing drinks category; typical of the asset-light strategy of the Kent and Quincey years.

title: Three European bottlers to merge into Coca-Cola European Partners
what: On 6 August Coca-Cola Enterprises announced that it will merge with Coca-Cola Iberian Partners and Coca-Cola's own German bottler into a new company, Coca-Cola European Partners, which will be the world's largest independent Coca-Cola bottler. Coca-Cola is selling bottling operations around the world to concentrate on brands and concentrate.
why: Part of the move back to an asset-light model that raised Coca-Cola's margins in 2016-2018.

title: James Quincey to succeed Muhtar Kent as chief executive
what: On 9 December Coca-Cola announced that president and chief operating officer James Quincey, a 20-year company veteran, will succeed Muhtar Kent as chief executive on 1 May 2017; Kent stays chairman. Coca-Cola is in the middle of refranchising its North American bottling territories to independent bottlers, which shrinks its revenue but raises its margins.
why: Quincey ran the company for nine years and turned it into a 'total beverage company' with more brands beyond soda.

title: Coca-Cola buys Costa Coffee
what: On 31 August Coca-Cola agreed to buy the British coffee chain Costa from Whitbread for 3.9 billion pounds. Costa runs coffee shops in Britain and other countries.
why: Quincey's biggest deal, aimed at hot drinks, a category Coca-Cola had barely touched.

title: Pandemic closes restaurants, stadiums and cinemas: Coca-Cola falls 17%
what: As the coronavirus spread, governments ordered people to stay at home and closed restaurants, bars, cinemas and stadiums, and stock markets crashed. Coca-Cola sells a large part of its drinks through such places. Its shares lost about 17% in March, more than the S&P 500.
why: In April Coca-Cola said away-from-home channels made up about half its revenue and its volume had fallen about 25% since the start of April. The business recovered with the reopenings in 2021.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_stock_market_crash (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/21344/000002134420000011/a2020q1earningsrelease.htm (released 21 April 2020, used for hindsight only, read 2026-10-03)

title: Coca-Cola recovers from the pandemic and buys BodyArmor
what: Coca-Cola reported on 10 February that unit case volume grew 8% in 2021 and revenue 17%, with comparable earnings per share up 19%, as restaurants and stadiums reopened. In November it bought the remaining 85% of the sports drink BodyArmor for 5.6 billion dollars.
why: The pandemic dip was fully reversed; BodyArmor was the largest acquisition of the Quincey years.

title: Coca-Cola passes on inflation: revenue up 11% in 2022
what: Coca-Cola reported on 14 February that net revenue grew 11% to 43 billion dollars in 2022, with organic revenue up 16%, mostly from higher prices; volume rose 5%. Comparable earnings per share grew 7% despite a strong dollar. The company gained market share and bought the sports drink BodyArmor.
why: Shows the pricing power of the brand in the inflation of 2022: Coca-Cola shares rose about 7% that year while the S&P 500 fell sharply.

title: Higher prices keep Coca-Cola growing
what: Coca-Cola reported on 13 February that organic revenue grew 12% in 2023, mostly from higher prices, while unit case volume rose 2%; comparable earnings per share grew 8% to 2.69 dollars. Chairman James Quincey speaks of an 'all-weather strategy'.
why: The pattern of the 2020s: modest volume, strong pricing, steady earnings growth.

title: Henrique Braun to succeed James Quincey
what: On 10 December Coca-Cola elected its chief operating officer Henrique Braun, 57, a Brazilian-American who joined the company in 1996, as chief executive from 31 March 2026. James Quincey, CEO for nine years, becomes executive chairman. Under Quincey the company added more than ten billion-dollar brands.
why: The current chapter; the shares rose strongly in 2026, to a record month-end price of nearly 89 dollars in August.
